claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi and closely matched fcc high-entropy-alloy derivatives have coercive fields below or no greater than 100 Oe.
Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization.
Controlled aging can induce nanoscale intermetallic precipitates in an fcc FeCoNi matrix.
The aging treatment can specifically produce nanoscale L10-ordered precipitates in the fcc matrix.
Solutionizing at 1150–1200°C, quenching, and aging at approximately 500–600°C for several hours is a suitable processing route for producing the proposed precipitates.
The proposed heat treatment can retain an fcc matrix while forming the secondary precipitate phase.
Nanoscale L10-ordered precipitates act as magnetic domain-wall pinning centers.
The precipitates increase the energy barrier to domain-wall motion.
Increased resistance to domain-wall motion raises the coercive field.
Aged material will have greater coercivity than single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a matched quenched control.
The coercive field may exceed 100 Oe after aging.
High saturation magnetization can be maintained despite precipitation and aging.
The magnitude of coercivity enhancement depends on precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction.
TEM and XRD can be used to test for the proposed nanoscale precipitates and L10 ordering.
Room-temperature VSM can measure the coercivity difference between aged and quenched-control samples.

contradictions.description: The prediction only says coercivity may exceed 100 Oe, but the falsification rule treats remaining below 100 Oe as equivalent to lacking a statistically significant increase. A statistically significant increase relative to a lower-coercivity control could still remain below 100 Oe.

The conditions request low-frequency AC magnetic measurements comparable to prior studies, whereas the controlled experiment specifies room-temperature VSM without defining an equivalent field waveform, frequency, sweep rate, or other matching measurement protocol.
